item.title: Before your interview: sessions vs. JWT, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
item.description: Checking a password takes one line of code. The hard part is everything after it: how the server remembers, on the next hundred requests, that this browser belongs to a user who logged in. That is what this interview topic is about, and the questions come in a predictable chain: “session or JWT?”, then “where do you store the token?”, then “how do you log someone out?”, then “how does ‘Sign in with Google’ work?”. Each step has a popular answer that is half wrong.

item.title: Before your interview: XSS, CSRF, CORS and SameSite
item.description:
XSS, CSRF, CORS and SameSite come up in almost every web security interview, and rarely one at a time. The interviewer asks about one, then asks how it relates to another, because that is where shallow answers break: “CORS protects against CSRF”, “React prevents XSS”, “SameSite made CSRF tokens obsolete”. Each of those sentences is half true, and the missing half is exactly what the follow-up question is about.

The four fit together once you separate two questions the browser answers for every request: can this page make the browser send something? and can this page read what comes back? XSS is an attacker getting to run code inside the target’s origin, where both answers are yes. CSRF is an attacker abusing the fact that sending is allowed even when reading is not. CORS controls reading. SameSite controls whether cookies go along with the sending.

item.title: Before your interview: what happens when you type a URL, security edition
item.description:
“What happens when you type a URL into the browser and press Enter?” is the most common open question in web security interviews, for pentester, AppSec and security engineer roles alike. It sounds like a networking quiz. It isn’t one.

The interviewer wants to see two things. First, whether you can hold a whole system in your head, from a keystroke to pixels. Second, and this is what separates a security answer from a networking answer, whether you notice that every hop is a trust decision: something tells the browser where to go, something proves who is on the other end, and something decides what the page is allowed to do. Each of those can lie, and each has a control with a known limit.
